reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose vacuum before parts: with engine running, one line to the axle shift motor should read ~20 in-Hg and switch when the transfer case is shifted. Replace cracked vacuum lines and the vacuum switch first; replace the CAD actuator if the diaphragm is ruptured. A permanent fix is a cable-operated 4x4 Posi-Lok kit that eliminates the vacuum system. Parts $30-$200; typical repair $100-$400.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: There is no patch repair for a dropped seat. The affected cylinder head (often both) must be replaced or rebuilt with upgraded seats; if the piston or valvetrain is damaged, a long-block or complete engine replacement is required. Owners keeping a pre-2009 HEMI should avoid overheating, maintain the cooling system rigorously, and address any cooling-system weakness or persistent misfire (P0301-P0308) immediately. When replacing one head, many shops replace both heads plus the timing set and oil pump, which are also known weak points on this engine family.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose the tick with a stethoscope to rule out exhaust-manifold leaks vs. internal valvetrain. Confirmed lifter/cam failure requires replacing all 16 lifters, the camshaft, and often rockers/pushrods (and inspecting MDS solenoids). Many owners delete MDS during the repair. Stay on top of oil changes with the correct spec and avoid extended oil-change intervals; some run a slightly heavier oil to mask early tick. Document the failure for the class action if eligible.

Verify proper brake-pedal feel and warning-light clearance after repair.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Have the system leak-tested (UV dye or electronic sniffer) to confirm the condenser as the source versus a hose, O-ring or compressor. If the truck qualifies for the manufacturing-defect warranty extension, the condenser may be replaced at no/low cost; otherwise replace the condenser (verified Mopar PN 68322495AB / 68312697AC for 2019-2024 DT), evacuate and recharge the system, and verify with a pressure/leak test. Add a condenser guard if impact damage is a concern.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Confirm the leak by listening for a cold-start tick at the cylinder head/manifold area, checking for black soot trails, and inspecting for missing or broken manifold bolts/studs; a smoke test can help pinpoint smaller leaks. The proper repair is to remove the manifold, extract any broken bolts from the cylinder head, check the manifold for warping, and replace the failed hardware with updated bolts/studs and new manifold gaskets; if the manifold is warped or cracked, replace it rather than reusing it. Many shops replace both side bolts on the affected bank as preventive maintenance because thermal cycling commonly causes repeat failures. Typical repair cost is about $400-$900 for one side if extraction is straightforward, but can exceed $1,200-$1,800 if multiple bolts are seized/broken or manifold replacement is required.

Typical $100-$400 depending on module vs. key relearn.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Do the preventive 'wiggle test': with the engine off, grab the external power terminal (10mm bolt) and try to move it; any movement means the internal stud is loosening and needs immediate attention. Genuine Cummins intake air heaters (e.g., 3970000 / 3970001) are direct replacements but retain the original design.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the VGT actuator with a genuine remanufactured Holset unit (common OEM/service PNs for 2007.5-2012: 2837675 / 4034315HX / 4046534 / 4049828; later 2013-2018 trucks use the updated HE300VG actuator). The new actuator MUST be calibrated/aligned and programmed to the turbo with a Cummins-capable scan tool (wiTECH) or a pre-programmed 'corded' plug-and-play unit such as the BD Diesel corded HE351 actuator. If the vane mechanism itself is seized with soot the whole turbo may need replacement. Clean the vanes/EGR side and address coolant leaks that corrode the board to prevent recurrence.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the VGT actuator with a genuine remanufactured Holset unit (common OEM/service PNs for 2007.5-2012: 2837675 / 4034315HX / 4046534 / 4049828; later 2013-2018 trucks use the updated HE300VG actuator). The new actuator MUST be calibrated/aligned and programmed to the turbo with a Cummins-capable scan tool (wiTECH) or a pre-programmed 'corded' plug-and-play unit such as the BD Diesel corded HE351 actuator. If the vane mechanism itself is seized with soot the whole turbo may need replacement. Clean the vanes/EGR side and address coolant leaks that corrode the board to prevent recurrence.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Replace the front pinion seal AND the pinion flange sleeve (wear sleeve) together, not the seal alone, since a grooved sleeve will re-leak. Set pinion preload correctly on reassembly. Inspect the axle-tube/input shaft seals at the same time and replace if seeping. Use the correct gear oil and confirm the axle vent is not clogged (a plugged vent builds pressure and pushes oil past seals).

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Start with TCM software update at dealer (free under warranty), reference TSB 21-008-18 REV.C. Have dealer perform transmission adaptation reset after update. If shifts remain harsh, request valve body inspection/replacement ($1,200-2,000). Ensure correct ZF 9-speed fluid is used (Mopar 68218925AA). Complete fluid change (not just drain and fill) every 40,000 miles. If transmission has failed completely, replacement/rebuild costs $3,000-5,000. Some owners opt for remanufactured transmissions from Jasper or AAMCO.

If shifts remain harsh, request valve body inspection/replacement ($1,200-2,000). Ensure correct ZF 9-speed fluid is used (Mopar 68218925AA). Complete fluid change (not just drain and fill) every 40,000 miles. If transmission has failed completely, replacement/rebuild costs $3,000-5,000. Some owners opt for remanufactured transmissions from Jasper or AAMCO.
